title: Variational Quantum Optimization of Noisy Polarization Qubit Experiments
authors: Timur Javid, Brian Doolittle, Colin P. Lualdi, Brittany Conner, Michael Vayninger, Eric Chitambar, Paul G. Kwiat
abstract: Quantum networking enables advanced communication protocols, distributed quantum computing, and enhanced sensing. These applications are often hindered by current realizations of quantum network nodes, which utilize noisy and imperfect hardware. Here, we apply variational optimization to counteract the effects of such imperfections. We parameterize network protocols for use with variational methods and then use these methods to optimize simple prepare-and-measure protocols on an optical testbed as a proof-of-principle demonstration. We demonstrate automated polarization compensation, achieving results comparable to conventional methods. We also analyze the effects of hardware imperfections and dark counts on the performance of our optimizations. We compare the performance of various gradient estimation methods and propose natural extensions, including further improvements through the use of global optimization and hybrid gradient estimation methods, as well as the application of variational optimization to nodes deployed on fiber networks.
summary: This work demonstrates the use of Variational Quantum Optimization (VQO) to compensate for noise and imperfections in quantum communication protocols using polarization qubits. By optimizing preparation and measurement settings on an optical testbed, the authors show that VQO can effectively maintain high fidelity for tasks like state discrimination and Random Access Codes. This offers a robust, hardware-efficient method for realizing quantum networking in noisy environments.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of maintaining quantum information integrity in noisy quantum network nodes, particularly in optical fiber links.
main_result: Variational Quantum Optimization (VQO) successfully optimizes prepare-and-measure protocols, achieving polarization compensation comparable to conventional methods while analyzing the impact of hardware noise.
method: The authors employ VQO, a hybrid quantum-classical optimization technique, to maximize success probabilities for state discrimination and Random Access Codes (RACs) by tuning hardware parameters.
model_or_system: The system uses polarization-encoded qubits transmitted through an optical testbed simulating a quantum channel (CPTP map) susceptible to noise like birefringence. The protocol involves an encoder (Alice) and a decoder (Bob) using waveplates.
key_observables: Success probability for state discrimination ($P_{SD}^{	ext{Success}}$) and Random Access Codes ($P_{RAC}^{	ext{Success}}$), and the resulting average state fidelity.
important_parameters: Waveplate rotation angles ($\vec{	heta}$), noise parameters ($\omega$), and the number of encoded bits ($n$).
main_assumptions: The VQO methodology is designed to be hardware-agnostic, optimizing over controllable elements rather than assuming perfect channel knowledge.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the prepare-and-measure scenario setup, detailing the optical components (waveplates, PBS) used for the VQO demonstration.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the general noisy channel problem to applying VQO for state discrimination and RACs, comparing gradient estimation methods, and finally analyzing hardware limitations and proposing global optimization extensions.
why_interesting: It provides a practical, data-driven framework (VQO) for mitigating realistic noise sources in photonic quantum communication, which is highly relevant for experimental quantum optics and quantum networking research.
